You extract source evidence for a paper-derived scientific benchmark. Return exactly one JSON object matching the supplied schema, with no Markdown or additional text.

Use only the fixed, line-numbered source packet. Do not use outside knowledge and do not infer an omitted coefficient, exponent, range, experimental condition, or uncertainty convention.

Extract at most one relation: the best source-supported executable quantitative relation connecting one to five numeric controls to one or two numeric readouts. A second source-reported condition is not required. Do not construct a pair, alternate world, counterfactual, task prompt, or benchmark design. If the source contains no complete relation, return {"relations":[]}.

The relation has exactly six fields: formula, parameters, controls, readouts, domain, and anchors. Formula.outputs is an executable expression tree for the source-reported central relation. Output keys must exactly match the readout names. A var leaf names a declared control and a param leaf names a declared parameter. Every declared control and parameter must occur in the formula. Numeric literals are allowed only for structural zero and one; encode every other scientific constant or fitted value as an anchored parameter. Preserve equality, approximation, fitted-relation, and asymptotic scope through the applicability statements; do not turn proportionality without its coefficient, an inequality, or an unspecified function into an exact point predictor.

A control is a numeric independent variable that can be queried within the source-supported domain. A readout is the quantitative dependent variable returned by the relation. Do not turn a latent quantity or an unreported fitted quantity into a control. Use continuous_interval only when the source supports a finite interval with minimum below maximum. Use numeric_values only for at least two explicitly supported numeric values. The domain must name every control exactly once. Record source-reported applicability or fixed context when present; otherwise use an empty applicability array.

Every formula, parameter value, control definition, readout definition, control domain, and applicability statement must carry direct inclusive source line ranges. Anchors contain line_start and line_end only. Do not generate a paraphrased support field. Use the line coordinates exactly as supplied.

Do not output source identity, schema version, an assessment, readiness flag, mechanisms, claim dependencies, ambiguity records, budget, diagnostic conditions, held-out conditions, public prose, provenance mappings, or code. Source identity and all benchmark-design fields are supplied or generated by deterministic code.

L000072	\begin{abstract}
L000073	
L000074	Near the end of their lives, low- and intermediate-mass stars expel metal-enriched material in winds and outflows, ultimately producing planetary nebulae (PNe).\cite{kwok78,iben83} The ejected material is expected to fragment and mix into the interstellar medium (ISM), but this final assimilation step has been difficult to observe directly.\cite{borkowski90,wareing07}
L000075	Here we report evidence for this process in the form of twenty-two bow shocks in the eastern outskirts of the Helix Nebula, detected in H$\alpha$ emission with the partially completed MOTHRA telescope.
L000076	Unlike the large-scale wind--ISM bow shocks commonly observed around evolved stars,\cite{wareing06,Martin2007,Cox2012} the shocks are compact and associated with individual clumps of gas.
L000077	Going outward from the central star, the radius of curvature $R_{\rm c}$
L000078	decreases by a factor of $\sim 10^2$ over the radial range $r=0.4$--$1.4$\,pc.
L000079	This is accompanied by a morphological transition from thin, well-defined
L000080	bows to fuzzy, patchy structures.
L000081	We interpret these changes as progressive stripping and fragmentation
L000082	of AGB-shell remnants as they interact with the ISM.
L000083	The slope of the observed $R_{\rm c}$--$r$ relation implies a loss
L000084	of fragment coherence on a timescale of $\approx 10^4$\,yr, providing a rare direct constraint on the time-scale for disruption and entrainment of fragmented stellar ejecta into the ISM.\cite{klein:94,karakas14}
L000085	
L000086	
L000087	
L000088	\end{abstract}
L000089	
L000090	
L000091	
L000092	
L000093	The Helix Nebula (NGC\,7293) is one of the closest and brightest PNe, and therefore a benchmark for resolving how the late-stage ejecta of stars couple to their surroundings. Using the Gaia EDR3/DR3 astrometric solution for the central star (WD\,2226$-$210), we adopt a distance of $d = 198.6^{+1.6}_{-1.8}$\,pc.\cite{bailerjones21} Imaging of the Helix has shown it to be highly complex.
L000094	Its bright main nebula comprises an inner disk and a surrounding outer torus, embedded within a larger structure whose upstream side is truncated, consistent with interaction between the expanding AGB ejecta and the ambient interstellar medium (ISM).\cite{odell:04,meaburn:05,zhang:12}
L000095	The ionized nebula is threaded by thousands of dense cometary knots and associated molecular material, indicating that much of the ejected material remains in a clumpy, only partially processed phase.\cite{odell:04,hora06}
L000096	Deep imaging and spectroscopy have also revealed a bow-shock feature in the faint outer halo, in the direction of
L000097	the nebula’s motion through the local ISM.\cite{meaburn:05,meaburn:13}
L000098	Together, these properties make the Helix uniquely suited to place direct constraints on how fragmented stellar ejecta are dispersed and mixed into the ISM —- an essential step in the recycling of mass, dust, and newly synthesized elements in galaxies.\cite{wareing07,karakas14}
L000099	
L000100	
L000101	
L000102	
L000103	
L000104	
L000105	The Helix Nebula was observed in the light of
L000106	H$\alpha$, [N\,{\sc ii}], and [O\,{\sc iii}] with the partially-built Modular
L000107	Optical Telephoto Hyperspectral Robotic Array (MOTHRA).
L000108	MOTHRA is an array of high-end telephoto lenses equipped with tiltable
L000109	ultra-narrow interference filters, located at the El Sauce Observatory in
L000110	Chile. Its design evolved from the Dragonfly Spectral Line Mapper
L000111	at New Mexico Skies Observatory.\cite{lokhorst:24,chen:25}
L000112	When completed, MOTHRA will have
L000113	1140 lenses distributed over 30 mounts, and be
L000114	optically-equivalent to a 4.8\,m f/0.08 refractor.
L000115	The data described here are equivalent to $\approx 20$\,min
L000116	on-source exposure time with the completed array.
L000117	
L000118	The MOTHRA H$\alpha$
L000119	image of the Helix is shown in Fig.\ \ref{helix_ha_large.fig}. It shows
L000120	many features that have not been seen in ionized gas before, such as extensions
L000121	of the plumes in the northwest and southeast\cite{odell:04,zhang:12} and
L000122	turbulent and complex low surface brightness
L000123	H$\alpha$ emission in the southwest.\cite{zhang:12}
L000124	The most striking feature in the H$\alpha$ image is a forest of arcs and
L000125	partial arcs on the eastern side of the nebula.
L000126	
L000127	We identify at least 22 arcs on the eastern side, labeled $1-22$
L000128	in Fig.\ \ref{bow_fit.fig} in order of increasing distance from the
L000129	central white dwarf.  While the majority of the features appear
L000130	to be new discoveries, several can be seen
L000131	in previous GALEX and H$\alpha$ images.
L000132	Besides the large and
L000133	complex feature 14 this includes arcs 3, 10, and 13, among
L000134	others.\cite{odell:04,zhang:12,meaburn:13}
L000135	The arcs are undected in [O\,III] and faint
L000136	in [N\,II]; from the brightest region of arc 14 we measure
L000137	[N\,II]/H$\alpha = 0.06 \pm 0.01$ and [O\,III]/H$\alpha<0.015$ (2$\sigma$).
L000138	We also find faint arc-like features on the western side, at a similar distance
L000139	from the white dwarf as the much brighter ones in the east.
L000140	
L000141	
L000142	\begin{figure*}[ht]
L000143	  \begin{center}
L000144	  \includegraphics[width=1.0\linewidth]{_helix_ha_large.png}
L000145	  \end{center}
L000146	    \vspace{-0.3truecm}
L000147	    \caption{\small \textbf{MOTHRA H$\alpha$ imaging of the Helix nebula.}
L000148	The MOTHRA continuum-subtracted H$\alpha$ image is shown with an inverted
L000149	grey scale, emphasizing faint outer features. In the bright central
L000150	regions a combined Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and Kitt Peak 4m image
L000151	is superposed on the MOTHRA
L000152	data.\cite{odell:04} The HST image was generated from data in the Advanced Camera
L000153	for Surveys F502N ([O\,{\sc iii}]) and F658N (H$\alpha$) filters.
L000154	The arrow indicates the Gaia-determined direction of motion of the
L000155	central white dwarf with respect to the ambient gas.
L000156	The MOTHRA image shows many
L000157	features at large ($\gtrsim 1$\,pc) distances
L000158	from the WD that had not been detected in H$\alpha$ before.
L000159	The most striking of these
L000160	are numerous bow shocks on the east side of the nebula,
L000161	where AGB ejecta encounter the ambient ISM at supersonic relative velocities.
L000162	The colour Hubble Space Telescope\,/\,Kitt Peak
L000163	image is reproduced from NASA, ESA, C.\ R.\ O’Dell (Vanderbilt
L000164	University) and M.\ Meixner, P.\ McCullough and G.\ Bacon (Space Telescope
L000165	Science Institute).
L000166	   }
L000167	   \label{helix_ha_large.fig}
L000168	    \vspace{-12pt}
L000169	\end{figure*}
L000170	
L000171	Following earlier studies we
L000172	interpret the eastern features as bow shocks where expanding stellar ejecta
L000173	encounter the ISM at supersonic velocities.\cite{zhang:12,meaburn:13}
L000174	The velocity of the Helix with respect to the ISM is
L000175	$\approx36$\,\kms\
L000176	toward $95^{\circ}$ East of North in the plane of the sky and $\approx 27$\,\kms\
L000177	along the line of sight,\cite{meaburn:13,gaia_dr3}
L000178	for a combined ISM velocity of $v_{\rm ISM}\approx 45$\,\kms\ with respect
L000179	to the systemic velocity of the nebula. On the eastern side the
L000180	shock velocity is the sum of $v_{\rm ISM}$ and the
L000181	expansion velocity of the ejecta, $v_{\rm shock,e} \approx |v_{\rm ISM} + v_{\rm exp}|$.
L000182	On the western side the ejecta encounter a turbulent
L000183	post-shock wake that has passed through, and mixed with,
L000184	the PN, $v_{\rm shock,w} \approx |v_{\rm wake} - v_{\rm exp}|$.
L000185	The wake velocity is expected to be small with respect to the systemic
L000186	velocity of the nebula.
L000187	In the case of the well-studied AGB star Mira the processed gas being shed
L000188	from the bow shock into the immediate downstream tail lags the star by only
L000189	$\sim 10$\,\%;\cite{wareing07,Matthews2008} applying the same
L000190	scaling to the Helix gives
L000191	$v_{\rm wake} =0-10$\,\kms\ for the flow on the western side.
L000192	
L000193	Using the
L000194	\textsc{Mappings~V} code\cite{Sutherland2018} we derive
L000195	shock velocities on the eastern side
L000196	of $v_{\rm shock,e} = 80-90$\,\kms\ from the [O\,III]/H$\alpha$ and
L000197	[N\,II]/H$\alpha$ line ratios (see Methods).
L000198	Subtracting the $45$\,\kms\ ISM velocity gives an
L000199	expansion velocity of the ejecta of $v_{\rm exp}=35-45$\,\kms,
L000200	consistent with previously measured H$\alpha$ kinematics in the region
L000201	of the brightest bow.\cite{meaburn:13}
L000202	The implied velocity field around the Helix is shown in Fig.\ \ref{vfield.fig}.
L000203	
L000204	Near the E-W axis
L000205	the shock velocities are $\sim 80$\,\kms\ in the east and
L000206	$\sim 35$\,\kms\ in the west.
L000207	For these velocities,
L000208	shock models predict H$\alpha$ luminosities that are
L000209	1--2 orders of magnitude fainter in the west than in the east,
L000210	consistent with the appearance
L000211	of the bows on the two sides of the Helix (see Methods).
L000212	
L000213	
L000214	
L000215	
L000216	
L000217	
L000218	
L000219	
L000220	
L000221	
L000222	
L000223	\begin{figure}[ht]
L000224	  \begin{center}
L000225	  \includegraphics[width=1.0\linewidth]{vfield.png}
L000226	  \end{center}
L000227	    \vspace{-0.5truecm}
L000228	    \caption{\small \textbf{Velocities experienced by fragments.}
L000229	Schematic velocity field around the Helix, for a bulk
L000230	velocity with respect to the ISM of $v_{\rm ISM}=45$\,\kms\
L000231	eastward, a post-shock flow velocity
L000232	of $v_{\rm wake}=5$\,\kms, and a radial expansion velocity
L000233	of the ejecta of $v_{\rm exp}=40$\,\kms.
L000234	The highest velocities are found on the east side, where we see the
L000235	strong bow shocks.
L000236	
L000237

L000239	The scale of the image matches
L000240	that of Fig.\ \ref{helix_ha_large.fig}.
L000241	   }
L000242	   \label{vfield.fig}
L000243	    \vspace{-12pt}
L000244	\end{figure}
L000245	
L000246	
L000247	
L000248	
L000249	
L000250	
L000251	
L000252	The expansion velocity of $v_{\rm exp}=35$--$45$\,\kms\ implies a dynamical age of
L000253	the clumps of 20,000\,--\,30,000\,yr at $r\sim 1$\,pc, predating the formation of the
L000254	planetary nebula $\sim 12{,}000$\,yr ago.\cite{meaburn:08}
L000255	The material therefore most likely belongs to an older circumstellar envelope that
L000256	was ejected during the late AGB phase, and has now fragmented into many individual clumps.
L000257	This interpretation is strengthened by the fact that the bows lie at approximately the same
L000258	radius as the $\sim 40'$ outer \textit{WISE} 12$\mu$m halo, which has been associated with dust from an AGB wind.\cite{zhang:12}
L000259	Fast winds and outflows, with velocities that can exceed the canonical $\sim 5-20$\,\kms\ range
L000260	of the main AGB phase,\cite{hofnerolofsson:18}
L000261	are commonly observed during the late-AGB and early post-AGB
L000262	phases.\cite{balickfrank:02,sahai:01} These flows are often bipolar rather than
L000263	isotropic,\cite{bujarrabal:01}
L000264	which may explain why there appears to be a preferred
L000265	axis connecting the strong bows in the east / northeast
L000266	of the Helix to the weak bows in the west / southwest.
L000267	
L000268	
L000269	
L000270	
L000271	
L000272	
L000273	
L000274

L000294	
L000295	
L000296	We fit the bow morphologies with a range of functional forms:
L000297	parabolas, hyperbolas, ellipses, and Wilkinoids.\cite{Wilkin1996}
L000298	We adopt the parabolic fits
L000299	as our fiducial model, as they provide a reasonable
L000300	description of the data and retain the same functional form under projection.\cite{tarango:18}
L000301	Since many of the structures do not show a complete bow, and
L000302	some are broader and less sharply bounded than ideal
L000303	thin-shell bow shocks, we do not attach direct dynamical significance to the adopted
L000304	fit family itself. Instead, we use the fits to extract geometric quantities
L000305	(in particular the characteristic curvature scale), and use the
L000306	variation between fit families as an estimate of the systematic uncertainty.
L000307	The fitting procedure is detailed in the Methods section, with
L000308	the results shown in Fig.\ \ref{bow_fit.fig}.
L000309	Most of the 22 bows are reasonably well fit by a parabola, although the wings
L000310	are often closer to hyperbolic.\cite{tarango:18}
L000311	The brightest bow (14) is
L000312	more sharply peaked than the model curve;
L000313	inspection of the region near the apex shows that it is broken up in a complex
L000314	network of smaller shocks.
L000315	
L000316	
L000317	
L000318	\begin{figure}[ht]
L000319	  \begin{center}
L000320	  \includegraphics[width=1.0\linewidth]{bow_fits.png}
L000321	  \end{center}
L000322	    \vspace{-0.3truecm}
L000323	    \caption{\small \textbf{Parabolic profile fits to bow shocks.}
L000324	{\em Left:} Twenty-two complete and partial bow shocks are identified
L000325	in the H$\alpha$ image. They are
L000326	fit with parabolas, indicated
L000327	with the red lines (see Methods). Red dots indicate the foci of the
L000328	parabolas; these correspond to the expected approximate locations of the objects
L000329	that produce the shocks. The lack of H$\alpha$ detections near the foci indicates
L000330	that the objects producing the bows are largely neutral.
L000331	The bows are numbered according to the distance
L000332	of the apex to the central star. Two known features, the NE Object and the
L000333	NE Arc,\cite{odell:04}
L000334	are also marked.
L000335	
L000336	
L000337	
L000338	   }
L000339	   \label{bow_fit.fig}
L000340	    \vspace{-12pt}
L000341	\end{figure}
L000342	
L000343	The foci of the parabolic fits are indicated with red dots
L000344	in Fig.\ \ref{bow_fit.fig}. These are the approximate locations of the shell
L000345	fragments that produce the shocks,
L000346	although the exact location depends on the 3D orientation and shape
L000347	of the bows.\cite{tarango:18}
L000348	There is generally nothing visible in H$\alpha$, [O\,III], or [N\,II] at or near
L000349	these locations.
L000350	The lack of detected emission counterparts at most of
L000351	the inferred obstacle locations is consistent with the fragments being largely neutral.
L000352	Our observations thus represent a new observational window on the mixing of AGB\,/\,PN ejecta into the ISM, in which the fragments are identified not by their intrinsic emission but by the shocks that they drive.
L000353	
L000354	The nature of the bows changes systematically with distance from the white dwarf:
L000355	close to the star they are large, thin, and well-defined, whereas in the outskirts they
L000356	are smaller and fuzzier. To quantify this trend without assuming a particular
L000357	steady-state bow-shock solution, we characterize each structure by the radius of
L000358	curvature at its apex $R_{\rm c}$, as measured from the best-fitting parabola.
L000359	The relation between $R_{\rm c}$ and the distance from the white dwarf,
L000360	$r$, is shown in Fig.\ \ref{R0r.fig}.
L000361	The characteristic size of the bows decreases by two orders of magnitude
L000362	over the radial range $0.4\,{\rm pc} \lesssim r \lesssim 1.4\,{\rm pc}$.
L000363	A log-linear fit gives $\log R_{\rm c} = 0.34 - 1.59\,r$, corresponding to an
L000364	e-folding length of $0.27$\,pc.
L000365	
L000366	
L000367	
L000368	\begin{figure*}[htb]
L000369	  \begin{center}
L000370	  \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{R_c_r.png}
L000371	  \end{center}
L000372	    \vspace{-0.3truecm}

L000384	
L000385	Because $R_{\rm c}$ is a purely geometric quantity, it does not by itself specify
L000386	the detailed momentum balance within the flow.
L000387	It does, however, show that the spatial scale of the coherent bow-forming obstacle
L000388	decreases strongly with outward distance.
L000389	This geometric trend is accompanied by a systematic morphological transition:
L000390	the inner bows are thin and sharply bounded, while the outer structures are broader,
L000391	more irregular, and increasingly clumpy.
L000392	Taken together, these changes suggest progressive stripping and fragmentation of
L000393	the dense AGB-shell remnants as they interact with the ambient medium.
L000394	As material is ablated from the fragments and mixed into the surrounding flow,
L000395	the surviving dense heads become smaller and more porous, and a larger fraction of
L000396	the H$\alpha$ emission likely arises in fragment-associated, mass-loaded mixed gas
L000397	rather than in a geometrically thin, well-defined forward shock.\cite{Hartquist1986,Pittard2001,klein:94}
L000398	
L000399	In this interpretation, the bows are both signposts of the fragments and agents
L000400	of their destruction.
L000401	The shocks are powered by the relative kinetic energy of the fragments and the ambient flow,
L000402	and their presence implies ongoing momentum transfer, ablation, and mixing.\cite{Hartquist1986,klein:94}
L000403	Interpreting the radial locations of the bows, $r_i$, as a time sequence for outward
L000404	evolution, $t_i \approx r_i/v_{\rm exp}$,
L000405	the slope of the $R_{\rm c}$--$r$ relation implies a characteristic time scale for the
L000406	loss of coherent bow structure.
L000407	For the expansion velocity derived from the shock velocities in the east,
L000408	$v_{\rm exp} \sim 40$\,\kms, the curvature scale declines with an e-folding time
L000409	$\tau_{R_{\rm c}} \sim 7\times 10^3$\,yr.
L000410	We therefore infer that the bow-forming AGB shell fragments are disrupted on a
L000411	time scale of order $10^4$\,yr.
L000412	This estimate should be interpreted as the survival time of the coherent dense
L000413	fragment/bow system, rather than as a direct measurement of a specific momentum
L000414	or mass-loss rate.
L000415	
L000416	
L000417	
L000418	Classical AGB--ISM bow shocks such as Mira trace a single, wind-driven stand-off interaction centered on the mass-losing star,\cite{Martin2007}
L000419	and far-infrared surveys show that such global wind--ISM interaction structures are common around evolved stars.\cite{Cox2012}
L000420	However, these long-lived\cite{Martin2007} ($\sim 10^5$\,yr)
L000421	large-scale bows primarily map where the wind meets the ISM; they do not directly constrain how fragmented ejecta are ultimately assimilated.
L000422	In the Helix outer halo we instead resolve numerous compact bow shocks with no luminous source at their foci, implying that the AGB--ISM interaction has
L000423	fragmented into dense, line-dark obstacles that are progressively ablated and entrained. The $\sim 10^4$\,yr characteristic disruption time for the fragments
L000424	can therefore be interpreted as the relevant time-scale for recycling of late AGB
L000425	ejecta into the ISM.
L000426	
L000427	
L000428	
L000429	
L000430	
L000431	
L000432	
L000433	
L000434	
L000435	
L000436	
L000437	
L000438	
L000439	
L000440	
L000441	
L000442	
L000443	More broadly, stellar mass loss is a major channel by which galaxies recycle gas, metals,
L000444	and dust back into the ISM,\cite{LeitnerKravtsov2011}
L000445	yet the efficiency and duration of the final, fragment-driven AGB\,--\,ISM assimilation step
L000446	remain poorly constrained observationally.\cite{Martin2007,Matthews2013AJ}
L000447	Galaxy formation simulations therefore rely on subgrid turbulent mixing and diffusion prescriptions to represent unresolved transport.\cite{Wadsley2008,Shen2010,Rennehan2019}
L000448	Our empirically inferred $\sim10^4$\,yr disruption time implies that once AGB ejecta are fragmented and exposed to the diffuse medium they lose their coherent
L000449	identity rapidly, providing a benchmark for models of recycling and feedback.
L000450	
L000451	Our conclusions can be tested and extended in several ways.
L000452	The  Helix is a fairly typical PN,
L000453	and we should see similar fragment-driven bow shocks
L000454	in the outskirts of other PNe. Because of the steep relation between H$\alpha$
L000455	luminosity and shock velocity such features will be most readily
L000456	detected when the bulk motion of the nebula with respect
L000457	to the ISM exceeds $\sim 40$\,\kms. When more examples are found,
L000458	it will be interesting to see if the
L000459	mixing timescale depends on the shock velocities.
L000460	Such observations will be within easy reach of the completed MOTHRA. Furthermore,
L000461	by analogy with the molecular cometary knots in the
L000462	Helix,\cite{Huggins1992,Huggins2002,Matsuura2009,Hora2006}
L000463	the H$\alpha$-dark clumps whose presence is inferred from
L000464	the shocks
L000465	could be detectable in CO rotational lines and, particularly,
L000466	in the H$_2$ 1--0 S(1) 2.12\,$\mu$m line.

L000497	\subsection{Observations\vspace{0.3cm}\\}
L000498	
L000499	
L000500	The Helix Nebula was observed as a
L000501	commissioning target during the early construction phase of
L000502	MOTHRA. When completed, the array will comprise 1140 Canon 400\,mm f/2.8 II/III
L000503	telephoto lenses distributed over 28 narrow band mounts and 2
L000504	broad band mounts. Each narrow band mount has 38 lenses: 18
L000505	are equipped with an H$\alpha$ filter, 8 with [O\,III]\,$\lambda 5007$,
L000506	8 with [N\,II]\,$\lambda 6583$, and 4 are continuum filters. The widths of the ultra-narrow
L000507	interference filters are $0.71$\,nm for [O\,III] and $0.93$\,nm
L000508	for H$\alpha$ and [N\,II], corresponding to a velocity bandwidth of
L000509	$\approx 430$\,\kms.
L000510	The continuum filters, two for H$\alpha$ and [N\,II] and two for [O\,III],
L000511	are $\approx 90$\,nm wide with a $\approx 33$\,nm
L000512	notch in the middle at the location of the emission lines. These
L000513	filters therefore measure the continuum at the wavelengths of the lines, without
L000514	being contaminated by them.
L000515	
L000516	The observations reported here were obtained on November 16 and November 19--24 2025,
L000517	when the first five mounts of MOTHRA were operational.
L000518	As the number of active lenses varied during the observations
L000519	we express the exposure time as single-lens
L000520	equivalent (SLE) hours, that is, the exposure time multiplied by the
L000521	number of lenses that were in use during the observation.
L000522	In H$\alpha$ the on-target
L000523	exposure time was 172.5 SLE hours, corresponding to 20 minutes with the
L000524	504 H$\alpha$ lenses that the completed MOTHRA will have.

L000528	\subsection{Data Reduction\vspace{0.3cm}\\}
L000529	
L000530	The data reduction includes several steps that are unique to
L000531	the design of MOTHRA and its prototype, the Dragonfly Spectral Line
L000532	Mapper.\cite{lokhorst:24,chen:25}
L000533	The $\approx 400$\,\kms\ wide
L000534	interference filters are placed in front of the lenses,
L000535	and specific wavelengths are chosen
L000536	by tilting the filters. Owing to the large
L000537	($\approx 3^{\circ}$) field of view
L000538	the wavelength of the bandpass is not constant over the image
L000539	but varies as a function of the angular displacement of the target relative to the projected tilt axis of the filter, as well as the angular distance
L000540	to the optical axis.
L000541	As a result, the sky background is complex:
L000542	sky emission lines appear as broad bands in the image,
L000543	particularly at the large tilts that are used for Galactic objects.\cite{lokhorst:24}
L000544	For the Helix observations we obtained offset sky exposures in a circular
L000545	pattern around the science field to model the background. Bracketing
L000546	sky exposures were combined and subtracted from each individual science frame,
L000547	prior to combining the science data.
L000548	
L000549	A color image of the Helix is shown in Fig.\ \ref{col.fig}, created from
L000550	the [O\,III], H$\alpha$, and [N\,II] data.
L000551	It is well established from narrowband imaging and line-ratio mapping that the
L000552	morphology of PNe
L000553	varies strongly between different emission lines, with low-ionization structures often enhanced in [N\,II] relative to [O\,III].\cite{balick87,corradi96,goncalves01}
L000554	The Helix shows the same behavior in its central regions and faint outer halo.\cite{odell:04,richer08,vandesteene15}
L000555	In the MOTHRA images, the forest of bow shocks is relatively bright
L000556	in H$\alpha$ and is faint in [O\,III] and [N\,II].
L000557	
L000558	The final step in the data reduction is the subtraction of continuum emission
L000559	from the narrow band data;
L000560	this was done by matching the point spread functions (PSFs) of the two images
L000561	and scaling the continuum image to match the normalization of the narrow band
L000562	image. Remaining residuals were filled in with the {\tt maskfill} code.\cite{maskfill}
L000563	The depth of the images was determined with the {\tt sbcontrast} method,
L000564	which empirically determines the contrast sensitivity on a desired spatial
L000565	scale.\cite{keim:22} The reduced and sky-subtracted narrow band images
L000566	reach a $1\sigma$ depth of
L000567	$\approx 2\times 10^{-19}$\,erg\,s$^{-1}$\,cm$^{-2}$
L000568	in H$\alpha$ on $1'$ scales.

L000580	\subsection{Shock velocity\vspace{0.3cm}\\}
L000581	
L000582	To interpret the observed emission-line ratios we compute a grid of radiative shock models using the MAPPINGS~V code.\cite{Sutherland2018} The models are run with Solar abundances and include a self-consistent treatment of the photoionizing precursor, in which the upstream ionization and temperature structure are iteratively determined from the radiation field produced in the post-shock cooling zone.
L000583	We adopt a pre-shock hydrogen density of $n_{\rm H} = 5~\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, consistent with the fiducial density used in recent MAPPINGS~V benchmark calculations\cite{Jin:25}, and appropriate for diffuse circumstellar and interstellar environments. The results are insensitive to the choice of $n_{\rm H}$, as the lines form when much higher densities
L000584	are reached.
L000585	The magnetic field strength is parameterized through $\alpha \equiv B/\sqrt{n_{\rm H}}$ (with $B$ in $\mu$G and $n_{\rm H}$ in cm$^{-3}$), which controls the degree to which magnetic pressure limits compression in the post-shock cooling zone.\cite{Sutherland2018}
L000586	
L000587	
L000588	
L000589	We explore two representative regimes: a weak-field case with $\alpha = 1$, which effectively captures the hydrodynamic limit (the results are virtually identical for all
L000590	values $\alpha \lesssim 1$), and a magnetically supported case with $\alpha = 2$, for which magnetic pressure significantly reduces the maximum compression.
L000591	Shock velocities are sampled finely in the range $v_{\rm shock} =20-115$\,\kms\ to resolve the transition in ionization structure associated with the onset of [N\,II] and
L000592	[O\,III] emission.
L000593	
L000594

L000678	\subsection{H$\alpha$ luminosity as a function of shock velocity\vspace{0.3cm}\\}
L000679	
L000680	There is a clear asymmetry in the brightness of shocks in the outer Helix nebula,
L000681	with all strong shocks located on the eastern side. As can be seen in
L000682	Figs.\ \ref{helix_ha_large.fig} and \ref{col.fig} There does appear to be a corresponding
L000683	region on the other side of the nebula, showing rounded arcs and bubbles
L000684	that are only detected in H$\alpha$. In Fig.\ \ref{east_west.fig} we show a side by side
L000685	comparison of the two regions.
L000686	Here we ask whether the difference in brightness
L000687	between the eastern and western shocks can be explained by the difference of the
L000688	shock velocities.
L000689	
L000690	The right panel of Fig.\ \ref{east_west.fig} shows the H$\alpha$ luminosity as a
L000691	function of shock velocity, from the MAPPINGS~V code.\cite{Sutherland2018}
L000692	At low velocities, the H$\alpha$ luminosity rises steeply with shock velocity as the shock progressively ionizes neutral hydrogen. At higher velocities, once the radiative precursor pre-ionizes the upstream gas, the hydrogen ionization fraction approaches unity and the
L000693	H$\alpha$ emissivity no longer tracks the mechanical energy flux. Instead, additional energy is channeled into heating and metal-line cooling, resulting in a flattening of the
L000694	H$\alpha$–velocity relation.
L000695	
L000696	Grey bands show the inferred shock velocities, $85\pm 5$\,\kms\
L000697	on the east side and $35\pm 10$\,\kms\ on the west side (see main text).
L000698	Because of the steep rise of the H$\alpha$\,--\,$v_{\rm shock}$ relation
L000699	in this regime, the H$\alpha$
L000700	luminosity is expected to be 1--2 orders of magnitude higher on the east side than
L000701	on the west side. The difference in the
L000702	observed surface brightness is a factor of $\sim 10$, broadly consistent with the
L000703	shock models.
L000704	
L000705	We note that the H$\alpha$ features on the west side are probably not
L000706	related to the
L000707	high velocity jet in that region, even though they appear to be in front
L000708	of it in projection (see Fig.\ \ref{east_west.fig}). The jet has
L000709	a velocity of $\sim 300$\,\kms, measured directly from H$\alpha$ and
L000710	[N\,II] spectroscopy,\cite{meaburn:13} and
L000711	if the shocks were driven by the jet they would show strong [O\,III] emission.

L000717	\subsection{Fitting of bow shocks\vspace{0.3cm}\\}
L000718	
L000719	The bows are fit in the following way.
L000720	A bow is initially characterized by
L000721	five manually-selected ($x$,$y$) positions:
L000722	two marking the end points of the visible arc,
L000723	one marking the approximate apex, and two points in between the end points and
L000724	the apex. Next, a second-order polynomial is fit to these five points. This
L000725	fit provides a reasonable approximation of the area of the image where the bow
L000726	is located. A band of typical width $\pm 20$ pixels is defined around the
L000727	polynomial fit. Within this band the
L000728	ridge of the bow is identified by determining the local maximum in bins along
L000729	the polynomial. To enhance contrast,
L000730	an unsharp-masked version of the H$\alpha$ image is used to measure the ridge.
L000731	
L000732	With the ridge line measurements in place,
L000733	a fit to an analytic function is
L000734	performed. Following earlier work,\cite{tarango:18} we fit four families of
L000735	functions: parabolas, hyperbolas, ellipses, and Wilkinoids.\cite{Wilkin1996}
L000736	For each functional form we determine the associated radius of curvature $R_{\rm c}$
L000737	and the related distance between the apex and the object $R_0$.
L000738	For a parabola $R_0 = R_{\rm c}/2$; for a hyperbola and an ellipse $R_0 =
L000739	R_{\rm c}/(1+e)$, with $e$ the ellipticity, and for a Wilkin profile
L000740	$R_0 = 3 R_{\rm c}/5$.
L000741	The five manually selected points are not used
L000742	in the fit. After the initial fit the band is redefined, now based
L000743	on the specific analytic function rather than the polynomial, and the ridge line measurements
L000744	and fit are repeated.
L000745	The process is illustrated for eight of the bows in Fig.\ \ref{fit_examples.fig}.
L000746	The fits are stable for the 22 bows that we identify in the image.
L000747	
L000748	As discussed in the main text, we use the parabola as the fiducial profile, and
L000749	take the rms ranges in $R_{\rm c}$ and $R_0$ from the four fits as uncertainties.
